Senses.Explanation: “When the form is straight, the shadow is upright” (形直影端) states a regular correspondence between an object’s shape and the shadow it casts. The Record of the Mirror of the School places it after “the sound accords and the echo follows” while arguing that differing appearances follow differing activity. Liao’an Qingyu applies the formula to the National Teacher’s three calls and the attendant’s three responses, before marking a later discrepancy. Zixianjue contrasts high “sound and echo” with low “form and shadow”; a later case compilation quotes Nantang Yu making the same assessment of the calls and responses. Miyun Yuanwu includes both paired correspondences in an address on coming and going. Another address rejects merely talking of these correspondences without the required action.

Senses.Explanation: A tight barrier or secured pass: a checkpoint represented as shut against passage and therefore as something to hold, close, break, or get through. In Luopu Yuanan's recorded formula, the last phrase first reaches this barrier, which shuts the critical crossing so that neither ordinary nor sage passes. Yuanwu Keqin repeats the same formula. The records also make the image operational: Puming holds the barrier shut through a ninety-day restriction period and then breaks it open; Baiyu Jingsi holds it with no inside or outside; Juelang Daosheng asks for the phrase that gets free of it. When an unnamed monk asks Tianyin Yuanxiu what the barrier is, Tianyin answers, "Break through it and come meet me." Senses.Explanation: An alms bowl is the monk’s concrete food vessel, but Chan speakers repeatedly make its familiar shape and capacity do argumentative work. Weilin Daopei calls up a lacquered bowl that contains the myriad things while being neither solidly real nor empty. Foyan Qingyuan mocks passive looking with a Yangzhou bowl that has impossibly grown a handle. Dahui Zonggao contrasts an ocean-sized capacity with bringing only a bowl and carrying away the little it holds. Yunmen Wenyan turns the bowl and its utensils into a blunt concrete command: remove the spoon and chopsticks from inside it. These images stretch the bowl’s capacity or fittings without changing the referent into an abstract substance.

Senses.Explanation: A monastery steward is the resident officer who handles a monastery’s practical affairs and answers for the institution in ordinary encounters. The role appears beside the named teaching figure and assembly rather than as another name for the abbot. Mazu’s steward asks after his illness; Yaoshan’s steward carries the assembly’s request for instruction. Linji questions a steward returning from selling the monastery’s yellow rice. At Wutai a steward asks whether Huihui bows to another or to himself; in the Pei Xiu case the steward answers for a temple’s wall image, and another temple steward answers an official about its protector image. The Danxia case makes the office’s custodial stake comic and sharp: Danxia burns a wooden buddha, and the steward who objects is said to lose his eyebrows. The Chan bend is the practical office entering famous public cases as the institution’s immediate custodian and interlocutor.

Senses.Explanation: The face or face-front: a bodily front imagined as a gate or opening. The graphs join 'face' (面) to 'gate or opening' (門), and the compound is attested. Its physical reference is explicit when Baozhi uses a finger to split open his face (以指𠢐面門) and when a fire-mass is said to scorch the face of anyone who comes near (近著即燎却面門). The record also uses verbs of impact with it: ‘press through the face’ (拶破面門) is attested, while ‘scorch the face’ (燎却面門) has 53 in 34. In the repeatedly quoted Linji case, ‘the true person of no rank’ (無位真人) is said to be constantly entering and leaving through the faces of the people present (常在汝等諸人面門出入); ‘entering and leaving through the face’ (面門出入) occurs 246 times in 157 source files representing 154 works. Yuanwu also records ‘a dynamic at the face’ (面門一機) in a small address and tells his interlocutor that he remains unaware even when it has ‘pressed through his face’ (拶破面門). These are the attested bodily, spatial, and case-specific uses; the texts do not supply a separate abstract definition for the compound.

Senses.Explanation: “Before donkeys and behind horses” pictures someone caught in a train of beasts, following rather than standing independently. Runguangze Zhengjue joins it to memorizing received formulas without knowing, and Yunmen Mailanghuai applies it to mistaken claims about understanding. Shending Feng says a conventional discussion of knowing and repaying kindness falls there, while Xisou Shaotan uses the phrase as the abrupt close of a hall verse. Yulin Tongxiu gives it as a direct reply to a monk who says he does not understand. A lamp witness preserves Dongshan Liangjie’s historically important warning that people mistake what they recognize before donkeys and behind horses for their own master of the house.
